newsitem.title: USA: Dollar closes weaker in U.S. amid EMU jitters.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes weaker in U.S. amid EMU jitters.

text.p: The dollar ended lower against the mark as comments by German and Italian officials fueled growing doubts that single European currency will be launched as planned in 1999, experts said.
The dollar also weakened versus sterling despite fading hopes for higher official interest rates in Britain.

In an interview with a German weekly newspaper this weekend, the German government's top independent economic adviser, Herbert Hax, urged Germany to put off joining the single currency until Germany's own finances were in order.
Hax also said Germany would likely fail to meet the entry standards on budget deficits and national debt this year.
By contrast, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Saturday told a tourism fair in Berlin that Germany would fulfill the criteria and the single currency would start on time.
The mark gained, as skepticism about plans for the euro tends to enhance its appeal as a safe haven currency.

That has been one of the factors that has allowed the mark to strengthen against the dollar in the last 24 hours, said Frank Pusateri, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Mellon Bank in Boston.

"It almost sounds like the more adamant Chancellor Kohl speaks about how there will be no divergence from the timetable or criteria ... the more it's obvious that Germany is not going to make it and they're going to have to delay the entry," Pusateri added.

Under the single-currency entry criteria spelled out in the Maastricht Treaty, nations must cut their budget deficits to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and public debt to 60 percent of GDP.
The German government forecast calls for a budget deficit of 2.9 percent in Germany in 1997.

Yet according to the text of a speech released Monday, Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher doubted the government would reach its goal, though he stopped short of suggesting the single currency should be delayed.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini added to the EMU pessimism when he told reporters this past weekend that he did not rule out a delay to the decision on who should qualify.
A decision on which nations will be included as founding members is scheduled to be made early next year.
The dollar ended at 1.7010/20 marks, down from 1.7058/63 marks at the open.
The dollar closed at 121.60/70 yen, down marginally from 121.72/77 yen at the open.
A British government report released on Monday showed Britain's factory output prices rose in February at their slowest rate in over a decade.
The data underscored Bank of England Governor Eddie George's comments earlier in the day that Britain's 2.5 percent inflation goal was within reach.
Initially, the British pound slid as low as $1.5948 before erasing it losses to trade as high as $1.6059 in New York. The pound ended at $1.6040/47, up from $1.5978/88 at the open.

Sterling fell because of the good inflation data and further erosion of expectations on UK interest rate hikes, said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
The pound rebounded after some traders who previously had sold the currency rushed to buy it back, while others thought sterling offered good value below $1.60, dealers said.

Elsewhere, the dollar fell to 1.4710/20 Swiss francs from 1.4725/35 at the open, but rose to Canadian $1.3712/17 from C$1.3706/11. The Australian dollar ended at $0.7888/93, up from $0.7863/68. ((-- Donna Sells, 212-859-1668))
